p.x:
Every country has different ideas about clothes. In Thailand, students usually wear a uniform: boys wear a white shirt and dark trousers or shorts, and girls wear a white shirt and a dark blue or black skirt. At university, many students still wear a uniform, but on Fridays some wear casual clothes, like jeans and a T-shirt, to show their own style.
Office workers often wear smart clothes. Men wear a shirt and sometimes a tie, and women wear a dress or a skirt with a blouse. In the rainy season, people carry an umbrella and wear shoes that are easy to dry, not leather boots.
When Thais travel to cold countries, they need a warm jacket, a hat and gloves. My cousin went to Japan in January. She said, "I wore three sweaters, but I was still cold! Next time I'll buy a big coat with deep pockets for my hands." Her favourite colour is pink, so of course the coat will be pink!

Two years ago, I made a decision: no more new clothes. Instead, I buy everything second-hand, from markets, charity shops and online. People often ask me why.
First, it's cheaper. Last month I found a designer jacket with the original label still inside for just 500 baht. In a shop, it would cost twenty times that. Second, the fabric is often better. Older clothes were usually made of natural materials like cotton and wool, and they were made to last.
I also enjoy creating my own look instead of following every new trend or buying whatever is fashionable. I think about what suits me and what matches the clothes I already have. Accessories like scarves and belts can completely change an outfit. Sometimes I have to make small changes, for example shortening a sleeve, but that's part of the fun.
Of course, there are disadvantages. Finding the right size can take a long time, and you can't always return things. But I've saved money, and I feel good knowing that I'm not adding to the mountain of clothes that are thrown away every year.

p.t: The Hidden Price of Fast Fashion
p.x:
Fast fashion has transformed the way we dress. Global brands now release new collections every few weeks, offering mass-produced garments at astonishingly low prices. A T-shirt can cost less than a cup of coffee. But who really pays?
Much of the clothing is made in countries where labour is cheap, and investigations have uncovered sweatshop conditions: long hours, unsafe buildings and wages too low to live on. The environmental impact is also enormous. The textile industry uses huge amounts of water, and synthetic fibres such as polyester release tiny plastic particles every time they are washed. Because cheap clothes are rarely durable, they are often thrown away after only a few wears.
In response, a growing movement is calling for more ethical fashion. Some consumers now buy fewer, better-quality items and choose versatile pieces that can be worn in many ways. Others turn to vintage shops or have clothes tailored to fit them perfectly, so they will be worn for years. Critics point out that these options are often more expensive. Still, as one designer puts it, "The most flattering outfit is the one you already own."
